title: Vampire Planet: California’s Water Wars Rage On
author: Joshua Frank
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_2229-680x564.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/07/californias-
water-wars-rage-on/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screen-
Shot-2026-08-06-at-1.14.37-PM-680x523.png)

Mono Lake, photo by Joshua Frank, August 3, 2026.

I just returned after a few days of hiking in California’s Eastern Sierra,
home to the Lower 48’s highest peak (Mt. Whitney, 14,405 feet), alpine lakes,
hot springs, and expansive valleys. It’s one of the state’s most scenic places
and, depending on when you ask, my favorite refuge from the steamy sprawl of
Los Angeles.

While much of the Rocky Mountain West experienced extremely low snowpack this
year, the Eastern Sierra didn’t fare well either, despite early rains in
December and January. It also saw low precipitation, with snowfall at
[24%](https://ladwpnews.com/2026-27-water-supply-forecast-below-average-
snowpack-levels-proactive-water-management-underway/) of its average annual
amount. Summer temperatures have scorched the Sierras. Thus far in 2026,
California has experienced its [warmest year on
record](https://www.facebook.com/reel/1286669693315140), and no corner of the
state has been spared.

This isn’t great news for the strange and beautiful Mono Lake, an ancient
saline lake with scattered [tufa
towers](https://www.monolake.org/learn/aboutmonolake/naturalhistory/tufa/)
along the western edge of the Great Basin. Since 1941, Los Angeles, 330 miles
south, has diverted water that feeds Mono, and that water now accounts for 2%
of the city’s supply.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_2229-680x564.jpeg)

The moon rises above Mono Lake, photo by Joshua Frank, August 3, 2026.

LA’s thirst nearly destroyed Mono Lake, which [lost half its volume
and](https://www.monolake.org/learn/aboutmonolake/savingmonolake/) dropped 45
feet. Toxic dust began to swirl, and gulls’ nesting grounds disappeared. It
wasn’t until the mid-1970s that a group of ragtag students from UC Davis and
Stanford stepped in and conducted a study showing that Mono was teeming with
life – a biological haven for brine shrimp and the birds that fed on them.
Despite their findings, ecological collapse seemed inevitable as long as Los
Angeles continued to draw water from the Mono Basin.

By the early 1980s, a movement to protect Mono Lake had grown, and in 1982 the
California Supreme Court ruled that the state must recognize its ecological
importance, overriding the city's alleged water rights. In 1994, the State
Water Board set legal rules requiring Los Angeles to reduce its draw from the
resources feeding the lake until it rebounded. The board set the water level
at [6,392 feet](https://www.monolake.org/today/2026-2027-mono-lake-level-
forecast-report/) above sea level. As of today, Mono Lake sits at around
[6,382.7 feet](https://www.monolake.org/learn/stateofthelake/), below the
state-regulated benchmark but still above its record low of [6,372
feet](https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/waterrights/water_issues/programs/mono_lake/docs/monolakedecision_presentation.pdf)
back in 1982.

Yeah, it's an improvement, but LA is still drawing too much water from the
basin. Mono still has a long way to go before it reaches the level scientists
consider healthy. The situation is far worse in Owens Valley, which lies south
of Mono Lake and [supplies one-third](https://healthebay.org/exploring-las-
water-legacy-in-the-owens-valley/) of Los Angeles’s water.

Since 1913, Los Angeles has been draining the Owens Valley, a process William
Mulholland conceived when he proposed building a viaduct to deliver water to
the burgeoning city. “There it is, take it,” Mulholland infamously said as he
watched the first stream of water flow through his new channel. Today, the Los
Angeles Aqueduct delivers an average of [430 million
gallons](https://www.monobasinresearch.org/images/2013AqueductCentennialFactSheet.pdf)
of water to the LA region every day, and it has left much of the Owens Valley
ecologically devastated.

Owens Lake (_Patsiata_ in the Native Nüümü, Owens Valley Paiute language) was
once a flourishing alkali wetland, but it is now nearly vanished. Invasive
plants have taken over, and the once-rich biodiversity has been destroyed.
Creeks have dried up, and streams no longer flow. The valley is a dust bowl
for most of the year. This environmental disaster falls squarely on the Los
Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP), which owns
[90%](https://www.ladwp.com/who-we-are/ladwp-eastern-sierra/owens-valley-real-
estate) of the private land in Owens Valley.

LADWP's land acquisition was a parcel-by-parcel land theft that was one of the
storylines of Roman Polanski's _Chinatown_ , and now, with climate chaos
further straining Owens Valley, those old California water wars are being
revived. A major legal victory for Owens Valley, particularly for Native
tribes there, came after LADWP faced a series of lawsuits and regulations
requiring the agency to conduct dust mitigation in the dry Owens Valley, which
the EPA has stated is the country's [largest
source](https://www.hcn.org/issues/issue-177/dust-settles-in-owens-valley/) of
particulate air pollution.

Now, organizations such as Friends of Inyo and the Owens Valley Indian Water
Commission have united to launch an initiative called Payahuunadü (the
Indigenous name for the Eastern Sierra). Their efforts aim to educate the
public about LA’s harmful water depletion in the Owens Valley and to hold
LADWP legally accountable. The ultimate goal is to restore this part of the
Eastern Sierra to its former thriving condition. Although Mono Lake’s recovery
is a modest success, Owens Lake could be an even greater achievement if it
comes to fruition. But they need our help. [Tap in to learn
more](https://ourwaterstory.org/).
